title: Concurrency, data races, deadlocks: blocking I/O under the OIDC store mutex, an unlocked binding writer, non-atomic refresh-family revocation, and quadratic memory-store paging

findings.title: memory.OIDCStore device decision holds the store-wide mutex across a durable audit write
findings.evidence:
func (s *OIDCStore) ApproveDevice(ctx context.Context, userCode, subject string, scopes []string) error {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	h, ok := s.userCodes[normalizeUserCode(userCode)]
	...
	s.devices[h] = d
	s.record(ctx, "oidc.device.approve", subject, d.clientID, audit.OutcomeOK)
	return nil
}

// DenyDevice:
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	...
	s.devices[h] = d
	s.record(ctx, "oidc.device.deny", "", d.clientID, audit.OutcomeDenied)
	return nil
findings.why: s.record calls s.audit.Record (internal/store/memory/oidc.go:349-360). The audit.Logger contract is synchronous and durable: audit/audit.go:35-39 says 'Implementations must not return until the event is durably persisted', and the shipped durable sink internal/store/postgres/audit.go:55-85 blocks on a committed batch (which also serialises on the chain-head lock). s.mu is the single global mutex behind EVERY OIDCStore operation - authorization codes, access/refresh tokens, introspection, userinfo, revocation, grants, sweeps. So while one device approval waits on a slow or stalled audit sink, the entire OP token plane is blocked behind it, with no per-store-operation deadline. This is an inconsistency as well as a hazard: every other write path in the same file releases s.mu before recording audit - CreateAccessToken (unlock at :546, record at :547), CreateAccessAndRefreshTokens (unlock at :658, record at :660), DeleteAuthRequest (unlock at :521, record at :526), CompleteLogin (unlock at :1279, record at :1282), RevokeGrant (unlock at :1474) - so only the two device methods couple the global lock to external I/O.
findings.exploit: A caller reaches POST /v1/device/decision (business plane) while concurrent POST /oauth/token requests are in flight. The audit sink is slow (pool exhaustion, chain-head contention, a paused SIEM endpoint). ApproveDevice takes s.mu, then blocks inside audit.Record; every concurrent token issue/refresh/introspection/userinfo blocks on s.mu until the audit write returns. A sustained audit stall turns a device approval into a process-wide OP outage.
findings.recommendation: Record the audit event after releasing s.mu, exactly as every other write path in this file does: move the s.record call below the critical section (drop the deferred unlock, unlock explicitly, then record), or record with a detached/bounded context. Do not call audit.Record while holding s.mu.

findings.title: federation.CompleteBind writes the vault secret and the binding row without the per-binding keyed mutex, so an in-flight bind can resurrect a just-revoked binding
findings.why: The per-binding keyedMutex (refresh.go:214-248) is documented as the mechanism that orders every writer of one binding's credential: Unbind takes it 'for the whole call' (unbind.go:41-51) so a refresh cannot write a secret back after an unbind shredded it; shredBinding takes it for the same reason (killswitch.go:195-202); CascadeRevoke takes it (revocation.go:128-133). CompleteBind is the one writer that stores a fresh secret (vault write) and then an unconditional Bindings.Put (the store's Put overwrites any Version), and it takes no lock. Therefore a bind callback that lands concurrently with Unbind / CascadeRevoke / RevokeUserBindings / RevokeAllBindings can re-create the binding row and a live upstream token AFTER the removal reported success. It also defeats the CAS ordering refreshBinding relies on: refreshBinding claims the row with PutIfVersion and only then writes the vault, all under the lock; CompleteBind's unconditional Put ignores Version and can replace or reintroduce the row underneath it.
findings.exploit: A user or an operator revokes a binding while an upstream bind callback is still in flight (two tabs, or a Kill Switch sweep running while a bind completes). Unbind/Cascade/shred finishes (row deleted, secret shredded), then CompleteBind's storeBindingSecret + bindings.Put re-creates the binding and a valid upstream credential. The user was told the source was disconnected and the operator was told the Kill Switch swept every binding, yet the source remains connected and usable. A compromised session can deliberately stage a bind and complete it after the victim runs the Kill Switch.
findings.recommendation: Take the same per-binding keyedMutex in CompleteBind for the whole store-and-put sequence (and re-read the row first, refusing to bind if the account has just unbound), or make the row+secret write a single compare-and-swap that a concurrent Delete invalidates. At minimum, write the row first with the store's versioned primitive and roll the secret back on failure, under the lock.

findings.title: Memory store pagers re-sort the whole table on every page: vault Rotate and the federation Kill Switch are O(N^2 log N)
findings.why: Each page call materialises ALL rows, sorts them, and only then applies the cursor as a filter. The cursor does not reduce the work. Rotation pages 200 records at a time (vault/rotate.go:96) and the Kill Switch pages 500 at a time (internal/federation/killswitch.go:99), so a run over N records performs ceil(N/page) full copies+sorts of N records: O(N^2 log N) time and O(N) transient memory per page. MemoryRepo.List also holds RLock for the whole sort/clone, so every concurrent Enroll/Revoke/Delete (vault writers) is blocked for the duration of each page; MemoryBindingStore.ListAllPage holds RLock while sorting, blocking Put/PutIfVersion/Delete. Both stores are the production backbone of the no-DATABASE_URL deployment (cmd/re0auth/main.go:897-898 constructs vault.NewMemoryRepo and federation.NewMemoryBindingStore).
findings.exploit: No attacker needed: an operator running a KEK rotation over a large in-memory vault, or the admin 'kill_switch' with target=bindings over a large memory binding store, spends quadratic CPU and repeatedly stalls all writers. With 100k rows a 200-row page loop is ~500 full sorts of 100k items. It is also a self-inflicted DoS during exactly the incident (key compromise / kill switch) where the operation must be fast.
findings.recommendation: Implement the cursor as a real keyset scan in the memory stores: keep or build a sorted slice/index once (or iterate the map and select only rows after the cursor with a bounded heap/sort of the candidates), so one page costs O(N + limit log limit) instead of O(N log N); or hold a pre-sorted snapshot outside the lock. The Postgres adapters already do keyset pagination - the memory twins should not be asymptotically worse. Also pass the caller's ctx through ListPage instead of context.Background() (vault/repo.go:233) so a cancelled rotation stops.

findings.title: federation.MemoryBindingStore.List has no per-user index: every account page scans all bindings under the read lock
findings.why: The store is keyed by a single string (user|game|source) in one map, so a per-user listing is a full scan of every binding in the deployment, held under RLock, on a hot authenticated read path. Every GET /v1/bindings and every GET /v1/account/export (which calls s.federate.Bindings) pays O(total bindings), and each scan blocks writers for its duration. This is the memory-mode production store (cmd/re0auth/main.go:898).
findings.exploit: As the deployment grows, each user's account page becomes slower in proportion to the WHOLE deployment's binding count, not their own; a burst of account-page loads serialises against every bind/unbind/refresh because the scan holds RLock. This is the classic N+1/table-scan shape the subject indexes in internal/store/memory were added to avoid for tokens (see its long comment at oidc.go:56-68).
findings.recommendation: Maintain a per-user index (map[account.UserID]map[string]struct{} or map[user][]key) updated inside Put/Delete under the same lock, so List is O(bindings of that user). Mirror the subjectIndex pattern already used by internal/store/memory/oidc.go.

findings.title: oauth.Service.Refresh: refresh-family revocation is not atomic with rotation, so a concurrent replay can leave the new generation alive
findings.why: ConsumeRefresh is atomic, but the sequence ConsumeRefresh -> RevokeRefreshFamily (on the reuse branch) and ConsumeRefresh -> issue (SaveAccess then SaveRefresh) is not. A replayed/stolen token (or a legitimate duplicate request, e.g. a client retry) racing the winning rotation can run RevokeRefreshFamily in the window between the winner's ConsumeRefresh and its SaveAccess/SaveRefresh: the family delete misses the generation the winner is about to mint, so the newly issued refresh token survives the RFC 9700 4.14.2 theft response. If RevokeRefreshFamily lands between SaveAccess and SaveRefresh, a live refresh token of the supposedly-dead family is left behind while its access token is gone. The production OP store (internal/store/memory/oidc.go CreateAccessAndRefreshTokens, :613-658) does the claim, the family revoke and both writes under one mutex, so this hole is specific to the oauth package path (used by internal/wiring and the reference/kit servers, not by cmd/re0auth).
findings.exploit: Two requests present the same refresh token: one is the victim's client retrying after a timeout (or a second tab), the other an attacker holding a stolen copy. Both pass TokenOwner (oauth/as.go:256). One consumes the token; the other gets the tombstone and revokes the family. If the winner's SaveRefresh interleaves after the revocation, the attacker's/victim's new refresh token remains valid despite the replay being detected - the family was 'revoked' while a live member of it was created afterwards. Conversely, benign duplicate refreshes can delete a session that was never compromised.
findings.recommendation: Hold a lock (or one store-level transaction) that spans ConsumeRefresh and the subsequent RevokeRefreshFamily/issue for the same family, so revocation cannot miss a generation minted concurrently. A per-family keyed mutex around Refresh (or a store method that atomically consumes, revokes on reuse, and mints) makes the theft response cover the generation actually issued. The OP store already does this; the oauth service should adopt the same shape.

findings.title: memory.OIDCStore replays and revocations scan every token and tombstone while holding the single global mutex
findings.why: All of these loops are full-map scans executed under s.mu, the one mutex every OP operation needs. revokeFamilyLocked is reached from TokenRequestByRefreshToken (:677-679) on a replay of a spent refresh token - i.e. from attacker-supplied input - and from CreateAccessAndRefreshTokens (:624-626). Every refundable scan blocks token issuance, refresh, introspection, userinfo and all other store reads for the duration, which grows linearly with the number of live tokens plus tombstones (tombstones live for the refresh TTL, up to 30 days).
findings.exploit: An attacker who has come by one spent refresh-token value replays it: TokenRequestByRefreshToken finds the tombstone and runs revokeFamilyLocked, an O(total refresh tokens + total tombstones) scan while holding the global lock. On a deployment with a large token table this is a cheap way to stall the OP for the duration of the scan, and unlike a rate-limited endpoint the work is proportional to server state, not to the request.
findings.recommendation: Maintain a family index (map[familyID]map[key]struct{}) and an idHash index, updated by putRefreshLocked/deleteRefreshLocked, so the family and paired-access deletions are proportional to the family size rather than the whole table. The package already keeps three subject indexes (oidc.go:56-68) for exactly this reason; family and idHash are the two remaining unindexed reverse lookups on this path.

findings.title: memory.OIDCStore.StoreDeviceAuthorization purges expired devices with a full scan under the lock on every call
findings.why: Every device-authorization request (POST /oauth/device_authorization, reachable by any client registered for the device grant) scans the whole devices map while holding the store's global mutex. The devices map has no upper bound enforced at insert - only a 10-minute TTL and the janitor's periodic sweep - so the per-request cost grows with the number of pending authorizations. The rate limiter bounds request rate per client, not the number of outstanding device codes a distributed or many-key client can create.
findings.exploit: A caller assembles many outstanding device authorizations (varied client keys/addresses, or one client if the limiter is generous); each subsequent device request then pays an O(N) scan under the global lock, adding latency to every OP operation on this store.
findings.recommendation: Cap the devices map (refuse new authorizations or evict the oldest) and/or amortise the purge: scan a bounded number of entries per call, or rely on the existing ticket-driven SweepExpired and delete lazily on lookup (a put does not need to purge at all). Keep the per-request critical section O(1).

findings.title: oauth.MemoryDeviceStore has no deletion path and no sweep, so device records grow without bound
findings.why: MemoryDeviceStore implements only SaveDevice/GetDevice/GetDeviceByUserCode/RecordPoll/RecordDecision. No method deletes a record: an approved, denied or expired device authorization stays in byDev, and its user-code entry stays in byUser, for the life of the process. The package's own MemoryStore has a SweepExpired (oauth/tokens.go:298) and is documented as needing an external loop, but MemoryDeviceStore has no equivalent and oauth.NewService never starts or exposes one; the service's DeviceStore interface (oauth/device.go:124-137) has no delete either. The device_code is not shown to the client after the response, so nothing else can clean it up.
findings.exploit: Repeated device-authorization requests (unauthenticated at the device endpoint for a public client) accumulate records and user-code mappings indefinitely; over a long-lived process this is a slow leak and every GetDeviceByUserCode lookup pays a larger map. Reachability is limited: cmd/re0auth does not construct oauth.NewService (it runs the OP store), so this store is used by internal/wiring and the reference/kit paths rather than the shipped binary.
findings.recommendation: Add a SweepExpired method to MemoryDeviceStore and a delete-on-decision (or delete-on-consume) step, and give the DeviceStore interface an expiry/sweep seam, mirroring oauth.MemoryStore.SweepExpired and internal/store/memory.OIDCStore.SweepExpired.

findings.title: readinessCache is not panic-safe: a panicking readiness probe latches /readyz to 503 'checking' forever
findings.evidence:
c.running = true
	c.settled = make(chan struct{})
	settled := c.settled
	c.mu.Unlock()

	probeCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), readinessTimeout)
	defer cancel()
	err := probe(probeCtx)

	c.mu.Lock()
	c.running = false
	close(settled)
findings.why: The state transition that clears c.running and closes c.settled runs only on the normal return path; there is no recover/defer around probe(probeCtx). If the deployment's ReadinessProbe panics, the panic unwinds past the unlock, leaving running=true and settled open forever. Every later /readyz then takes the 'a check is running' branch, sees state==readinessUnknown with a non-nil settled channel (health.go:163-168), waits the cold-start 500ms and answers 503 'checking' (health.go:130-138) permanently - a self-inflicted readiness outage that no dependency recovery can clear. The probe is also the one path exempt from the limiter and the in-flight cap, and each cold-start waiter allocates a fresh timer with time.After (health.go:175) that stays alive for the full 500ms.
findings.exploit: A readiness probe that panics (a nil dependency handle, a driver bug, an injected test hook) permanently takes the instance out of rotation with a misleading 'checking' body even though every request could be served. The waiters' timers are bounded per request, so the allocation cost is small.
findings.recommendation: Run the probe under a recover/defer that always sets c.running=false and closes c.settled (and records the panic as not-ready or keeps the previous verdict), so the cache state cannot latch. Prefer a reusable timer or a context deadline over time.After on the cold-start wait path.

findings.title: oauth.Registry.Register mutates a map that Resolve/Get/Descriptors read without any lock
findings.why: Register is documented as 'meant to be called at composition time', but nothing enforces it and there is no mutex. A Register after the server begins serving races every Resolve call made by /oauth/authorize, the device endpoint, the consent screen and oauth.Service; a concurrent map write is a Go runtime throw ('concurrent map writes'), not merely a data race. In the current composition root this is safe (cmd/re0auth/main.go:1318 builds DefaultRegistry once and registers nothing later), so the finding is about the exported API contract, not a live production race.
findings.exploit: A provider plugin that registers a scope after startup - exactly what the package doc invites ('provider packages will contribute their own descriptors as the catalog grows') - can crash the process or make a scope check see a torn value.
findings.recommendation: Either guard byScope with a sync.RWMutex (Register under write lock, Get/Resolve/Descriptors under read lock), or make registration possible only through a constructor and expose a frozen read-only type after New. Document the freeze in the type.

findings.title: oidchttp.serveOAuth can leak a pooled bufferedWriter on panic because release is not deferred
findings.evidence:
bw := acquireBufferedWriter()
	h.provider.ServeHTTP(bw, r)
	...
	bw.flush(w, body)
	releaseBufferedWriter(bw)
findings.why: The buffered writer is taken from the package-level sync.Pool (bufferedWriters, oidchttp.go:1605) and returned only on the normal path. If h.provider.ServeHTTP panics, the panic unwinds through serveOAuth (it is recovered by httpapi's recoverProtocol wrapper, not here) and releaseBufferedWriter is skipped, so the pooled buffer - which may hold up to 64 KiB - is dropped to the GC rather than reused. The request is still answered correctly; this is a pool-efficiency/latent-leak nit, not a correctness or data-exposure issue (no other request ever sees the abandoned buffer).
findings.exploit: None directly; a repeatedly panicking provider path simply defeats the pool and grows garbage.
findings.recommendation: acquire the writer and `defer releaseBufferedWriter(bw)` (copying out any bytes that must outlive it), or release inside a defer with the flush on the normal path.

findings.title: federation.refreshBinding's row-then-secret write order is deliberately protected by the per-binding lock (suspicious but mitigated)
findings.why: This looks like a row/vault divergence window: the binding row is committed with the new Version and expiry before the vault holds the rotated secret, so a concurrent reader could observe the new row while the vault still serves the previous token. It is mitigated: refreshBinding holds the per-binding keyedMutex across BOTH PutIfVersion and storeBindingSecret, and every other credential writer (Unbind, CascadeRevoke, shredBinding) takes the same key. A reader in trySource can read the new row and use the old vault token, but any forced re-refresh re-enters refreshBinding and blocks on the lock until the secret is stored, then re-reads the vault. The residual exposure is only 'a call uses the token that was valid a moment ago', which is not a lost update. Note this mitigation does NOT extend to CompleteBind, which takes no lock (S14-2).
findings.exploit: Not exploitable via this path: the interleaving that would lose the rotation is excluded by the per-binding lock. The union with S14-2 is the real risk.
findings.recommendation: Keep the lock spanning PutIfVersion and storeBindingSecret (add a comment naming CompleteBind as the reason it must not be dropped), and close the gap by making CompleteBind take the same lock.

coverage: audit/audit.go (contract and MemoryLogger, to judge lock-held I/O)
cmd/re0auth/main.go (storage wiring only: memory vs durable composition)

go test -race -count=1 ./internal/store/memory/... ./internal/ratelimit/... ./vault/... ./internal/federation/... ./oauth/... ./internal/oidchttp/... ./internal/httpapi/... ./internal/compress/... (all ok, no race reports)
go vet on the same packages (clean)
notes: Independence: only production code plus my own reasoning was used; AUDIT-ISSUES.md, docs/security-audit-*.md, internal/zzprobe/**, _audit/**, audit/** and scratchpad/** were not read as sources. The prescribed race run passed cleanly on all eight package trees (go1.27.1 windows/amd64) and go vet reported nothing, so every finding here is either a lock-granularity/ordering hazard the race detector cannot see, a quadratic/unbounded cost, or a genuine unprotected writer (S14-2). No true lock-order cycle was found: the per-binding keyedMutex is always the outermost lock on the federation paths and is released before any vault/repo lock; readinessCache releases its mutex before probing; the rate limiter and binding cooldown never take another lock while holding theirs. The most serious confirmed defect is S14-2 (CompleteBind not taking the per-binding lock that Unbind/Cascade/shred/refresh all take), and the clearest production-impact defect is S14-1 (the global OIDC store mutex held across a durable audit write). S14-5 is limited to the oauth.Service library path (not constructed by cmd/re0auth), and S14-8/S14-10/S14-11 are non-production/library or informational. Uncertainties: (a) S14-2's real-world severity depends on how often a bind callback overlaps an unbind/Kill Switch - the code path is unguarded but the trigger needs two concurrent user/operator actions; (b) S14-5's interleaving window is short but not eliminated, and I could not drive it deterministically without a store-level hook; (c) the Postgres OIDC/binding/credential adapters and internal/auth (session store) are outside this scope and were not audited, so a durable deployment's lock ordering may add cycles not visible here; (d) I did not read the vendored zitadel/oidc provider internals, so any concurrency defect inside the library (e.g. its device-consume order) is out of scope.
